items.question: What is the primary focus of Data Quality?

options.a: Making data look nice in dashboards
options.b: Ensuring data conforms to standards and meets business expectations
options.c: Storing more data than competitors
options.d: Reducing database storage costs

items.feedback_correct: Correct! DQ is about conformance to standards and business expectations.

items.question: Which DQ dimension refers to required fields being populated?

options.a: Accuracy
options.b: Completeness
options.c: Conformity
options.d: Uniqueness

items.feedback_correct: Correct! Completeness means required fields are populated with no critical nulls or gaps.

items.question: What is the correct order of the DQ lifecycle?

options.a: Remediate → Profile → Rule → Recheck
options.b: Profile → Rule → Remediate → Recheck
options.c: Rule → Remediate → Profile → Recheck
options.d: Recheck → Profile → Rule → Remediate

items.feedback_correct: Correct! Profile first to understand data, then Rule, Remediate issues, and Recheck.

items.question: What is the recommended maximum length for a rule name?

options.a: 50 characters
options.b: 85 characters (target); 100 characters (absolute max)
options.c: 150 characters
options.d: No limit; as long as needed

items.feedback_correct: Correct! Target ≤85 chars, absolute max 100 chars. Keep rule names concise and business-friendly.

items.question: What is the key difference between OptSel and RptSel?

options.a: OptSel returns errors only; RptSel returns all records
options.b: OptSel returns all records with error flags; RptSel filters to only errors
options.c: OptSel is for SQL; RptSel is for reporting
options.d: There is no difference; they are the same

items.feedback_correct: Correct! OptSel = universe (all records with flags), RptSel = wrapper (errors only).

items.question: Where do deletion flags (LVORM, LOEKZ) belong in a rule?

options.a: In the CASE statement that computes zIsErrorFlag
options.b: In the WHERE clause to exclude deleted records
options.c: In the SELECT statement as a column
options.d: Deletion flags are not used in DQ rules

items.feedback_correct: Correct! Deletion flags go in WHERE to exclude deleted records (they are out of scope).

items.question: Scenario: You're designing a rule for purchase orders. The business requires: "Every open PO must have a valid vendor reference that exists in the vendor master."

options.a: Completeness only (vendor field must be filled)
options.b: Completeness and Integrity (field filled AND vendor exists in the master)
options.c: Integrity only (vendor reference resolves to the vendor master)
options.d: Accuracy (vendor details are accurate)

items.feedback_correct: Correct! The rule tests both: (1) Completeness (vendor field must be filled) AND (2) Integrity (the reference must resolve to the vendor master).

items.question: Follow-up scenario: Where would you place the condition "EKKO.EKSTAT = 'OPEN'" in the purchase-order rule?

options.a: In the CASE statement as part of the error condition
options.b: In the WHERE clause as a scope filter (which POs to check)
options.c: In the SELECT statement as an additional column
options.d: Status fields should not appear in rules

items.feedback_correct: Correct! Status fields like EKSTAT go in WHERE to define scope (only open POs are in the universe) — scope filters live in WHERE, the error condition lives in CASE.

items.question: What happens if you define a CTE but never reference it in the outer query?

options.a: It's fine — unused CTEs are optimized away automatically
options.b: It's a dangling CTE — a sign of unfinished logic that must be fixed
options.c: It automatically becomes part of the Activity Context section
options.d: It replaces the need for a WHERE clause

items.feedback_correct: Correct! Every CTE must be joined or selected from in the outer query. A dangling CTE signals unfinished logic.

items.question: Which statement about zSourceSystemID is correct?

options.a: It only needs to appear in the outer query's WHERE clause
options.b: It can be written as a literal value like 'Z01' for simplicity
options.c: It must be filtered in the main table WHERE, paired in every join, and filtered/output inside every CTE
options.d: CTEs are exempt from zSourceSystemID filtering since they're internal

items.feedback_correct: Correct! zSourceSystemID filtering is mandatory in the main table WHERE, every join ON clause, and every CTE (both filtering internally and outputting the column) — CTEs are never exempt.

items.question: Scenario: A colleague submits this CTE for review:

options.a: Nothing — this CTE is fully compliant
options.b: The CTE doesn't output or filter on zSourceSystemID, and the join doesn't pair it either
options.c: The CTE should use a RIGHT JOIN instead of LEFT JOIN
options.d: CTEs should never use WHERE clauses

items.feedback_correct: Correct! The CTE must select and filter zSourceSystemID internally, and the outer JOIN must pair mara.zSourceSystemID = vendor_check.zSourceSystemID alongside the MATNR match — otherwise the join can silently cross source systems.

items.question: OptSel vs RptSel — Which statement is correct?

options.a: OptSel returns only error rows; RptSel returns all rows
options.b: OptSel returns all rows with zIsErrorFlag (1 or 0); RptSel wraps OptSel to show only errors
options.c: OptSel and RptSel are the same thing, just different names
options.d: OptSel is for performance; RptSel is for readability

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! This is the fundamental OptSel/RptSel distinction from Session 1.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Remember: OptSel = "universe" (all rows with flags), RptSel = wrapper (errors only). Crucial for Session 2.

items.question: zSourceSystemID Purpose — What does zSourceSystemID represent?

options.a: The date the rule was created
options.b: The SAP system (Production, Quality, Development) a row belongs to
options.c: The user who owns the rule
options.d: A random unique identifier for each record

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! zSourceSystemID identifies which SAP system a row belongs to.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Critical for Session 2. zSourceSystemID appears in four mandatory places in every rule. Review Session 1 before proceeding.

items.question: Deletion Flags Placement — Where do you put a deletion flag (LVORM, LOEKZ) check?

options.a: In the CASE statement that computes zIsErrorFlag
options.b: In the WHERE clause to exclude deleted records
options.c: In the SELECT statement as an additional column
options.d: Deletion flags should never appear in rules

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Deletion flags go in WHERE to exclude deleted records from scope.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Session 2 non-negotiable. Deletion flags are scope exclusions (WHERE), never part of error condition (CASE).

items.question: Error Flag Logic — Should the error condition go in WHERE or CASE?

options.a: WHERE clause — to filter out bad records
options.b: CASE statement — to flag records, not exclude them
options.c: Both — redundancy is safer
options.d: Neither — use a separate ERROR_FLAG column instead

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Errors in CASE (to flag), not WHERE (which is scope only).
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Core Session 1 principle. Error condition in CASE, scope in WHERE. Session 2 enforces strictly.

items.question: What is a CTE?

options.a: Comments Table Expression — used for documentation
options.b: Common Table Expression (WITH...AS block) — used to pre-aggregate or pre-filter tables before joining
options.c: They're required in every DQ rule
options.d: They're never used because they're too slow

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! CTEs are optional but powerful when used correctly.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ CTEs are optional. When used, Session 2 requires five specific rules. If new to CTEs, pay close attention to that lesson.

items.question: zIsErrorFlag Data Type — What should zIsErrorFlag always be?

options.a: Text: 'Yes' or 'No'
options.b: Integer: 1 (error) or 0 (clean)
options.c: Boolean: TRUE or FALSE
options.d: Decimal: 0.0 to 1.0 (probability)

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! INTEGER 1/0 is mandatory. Never text.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Hard Session 2 requirement. zIsErrorFlag must be 1 (error) or 0 (clean) — never text, never decimal.

items.question: Multiple Table Joins — If a rule joins two tables without zSourceSystemID in ON, what happens?

options.a: The SQL still works fine
options.b: The join might accidentally match rows from different source systems
options.c: SQL will automatically filter by system
options.d: zSourceSystemID isn't needed in joins

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Join without zSourceSystemID can cause silent cross-system leakage.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Major compliance issue. Session 2 requires zSourceSystemID paired in every join ON clause. Missing it = data leakage.

items.question: Status Field vs Deletion Flag — Identify which is deletion flag vs status field (LVORM, PSTAT)

options.a: LVORM = status, PSTAT = deletion
options.b: LVORM = deletion, PSTAT = status
options.c: Both are deletion flags
options.d: Both are status fields

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! LVORM deletes, PSTAT controls status.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Essential distinction. Knowing the difference is required for scoping rules correctly. Session 2 builds on this.

items.question: Multi-System Rules — You have rules for three systems (Z01, Z02, Z03). Should you:

options.a: Write one rule with WHERE zSourceSystemID IN ('Z01', 'Z02', 'Z03')
options.b: Write three separate rules, each filtered to its own system ID
options.c: Write one rule with WHERE zSourceSystemID = 'Z01' (hardcode it)
options.d: Use UNION to combine results from all three systems

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Separate rules per system ensure isolation and auditability.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Session 2 and Session 3 require system isolation. Each rule scoped to one system prevents data leakage and audits cleanly.

items.question: Field Section Order — What is the correct order for the five field sections?

options.a: Basic → Org → Value → Activity → Technical
options.b: Technical → Basic → Org → Value → Activity
options.c: Activity → Technical → Basic → Value → Org
options.d: There is no specific order

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Technical → Basic → Org → Value → Activity is mandatory.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ This order is enforced in Session 2. Every rule must respect it. Tested in "What a Good Rule Looks Like" checklist.

items.question: Rule Naming — Which rule name best fits Session 2 standards?

options.a: "Material data check routine for valid UoM assignment validation procedure"
options.b: "Matl must have valid BUoM"
options.c: "Material must have valid base unit of measure"
options.d: "mm_0042_check"

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Business-friendly, ≤85 chars, preserves acronyms.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Session 2 specifies exact naming rules. Rules must be readable by business users, not technical jargon.

items.question: Comment Standards — Session 2 says rule comments should:

options.a: Narrate every SQL line ("this selects the material number")
options.b: Explain business logic and non-obvious joins in plain language
options.c: Include performance tuning recommendations
options.d: Mention if the SQL was generated by AI

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Comments explain business logic for auditability.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Session 2 has detailed rules about comments. Comments make rules auditable — don't narrate syntax.

items.question: Literal System IDs — True or False: Hardcode zSourceSystemID = 'Z01' to keep SQL simple?

options.a: True — literals are simpler
options.b: False — zSourceSystemID must always be a column reference

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Literals defeat the filtering purpose. Always use column references.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Session 2 strict rule. Explicit prohibition. Literals cause silent data leakage bugs.

items.question: Deletion Flag in CASE — You see: CASE WHEN LVORM = 'X' THEN 1. What should you flag?

options.a: Nothing — checking deletion flags in CASE is fine
options.b: The deletion flag should be in WHERE (scope), not CASE (error condition)
options.c: Deletion flags should never appear in rules
options.d: The rule needs more CTEs

items.feedback_correct: ✓ Correct! Deletion flags belong in WHERE (scope), never in CASE (error condition).
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Core Session 1 → Session 2 principle. Common mistake. Focus on "Business Correctness" in Session 2's checklist.

items.question: You derive a rule with Local Derive, save it, then derive the exact same rule again next month with identical inputs. What should the resulting SQL look like?

options.a: Nearly identical, but comments and field order may vary between runs
options.b: Byte-identical to the first run — same structure, same comments, same field order
options.c: Different, because the derivation engine incorporates recent data profiling results
options.d: Different, because each derivation gets a new randomized view name

items.feedback_correct: Correct. Local Derive is deterministic — same input always produces the same output. That's what makes the SQL diff-friendly in version control and safe to certify for audit.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Local Derive is deterministic: identical inputs always produce byte-identical SQL — same field order, same comments, same zSourceSystemID placement. This is what makes rules reproducible and audit-ready.

items.question: AI Enhance returns rewritten SQL and the quality gate finds something serious in it (e.g. a hardcoded zSourceSystemID literal). What happens next?

options.a: The enhancement is silently discarded and the original deterministic SQL is kept
options.b: The Studio asks the AI once more, telling it what was wrong, then shows you whatever comes back with its findings attached
options.c: The rule is permanently locked from further AI enhancement
options.d: The consultant must manually re-type the entire prompt from scratch

items.feedback_correct: Correct. There is exactly one retry. Whatever comes back is recorded with its findings attached and shown to you, so the Reconciliation sheet shows what was caught. A finding means a human decides — it is not the Studio approving the rule.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ The gate retries once, telling the AI what was wrong, then hands the result back — clean or not — with its findings attached. It does not discard, lock or block; the short hard-stop list is the only thing that stops a save outright.

items.question: A conceptual rule fans out into three per-system implementations (P02, P03, P06). Which of these is shared across all three, rather than unique to each?

options.a: The DQOps rule_id
options.b: The view names
options.c: The SKP_RULE_NNNN and the rule's description
options.d: The zSourceSystemID filter value

items.feedback_correct: Correct. Rule name, domain/attribute/dimension, description, and SKP_RULE_NNNN are shared across siblings. Each implementation gets its own DQOps rule_id, view names, and zSourceSystemID filter.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ DQOps rule_id, view names, and the zSourceSystemID filter are all per-implementation — they must differ so each system's data stays isolated. What stays shared is the rule name, description, and the SKP_RULE_NNNN that groups the siblings together.

items.question: In the bulk pipeline's reconciliation table, a row shows status 'Failed'. What does that tell you?

options.a: The rule ran successfully and found a high volume of data errors (zIsErrorFlag = 1)
options.b: SQL generation for that rule did not complete — for example AI Derive hit a missing or rate-limited API key
options.c: The rule's RptSel returned zero rows
options.d: The rule was flagged by a client reviewer during audit

items.feedback_correct: Correct. 'Failed' is a pipeline-generation status, not a data-quality outcome — it means the rule never got as far as usable SQL. A rule that generated fine and then found lots of defects shows a normal status with a high error count, not 'Failed'.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Don't confuse pipeline status with data results. 'Failed' means SQL generation itself broke (a common cause: 'AI Derive failed' from a missing or rate-limited API key) — it says nothing about how many records the rule would flag once it has valid SQL.

items.question: You accept Claude's AI enhancement on the lead implementation (P02) of a multi-system rule and want it to reach the P03 and P06 siblings too. One sibling was already independently AI-enhanced with different logic. What does the Studio do with that sibling?

options.a: Overwrites it silently with the lead's new SQL, since siblings should always match
options.b: Skips it by default and reports the skip — it does not silently overwrite a sibling that has already diverged
options.c: Deletes the sibling implementation entirely
options.d: Blocks the enhancement from reaching any of the siblings, including the untouched ones

items.feedback_correct: Correct. Siblings are meant to stay identical apart from their system token, so propagation is the default — but a sibling that's already been independently enhanced or has diverged is always skipped and reported, never silently clobbered.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ The Studio propagates one enhancement across a sibling group to avoid re-running AI per system, but it protects against overwriting real work: an already-enhanced or diverged sibling is skipped and reported, not silently replaced. Untouched siblings still get the propagated fix.

items.question: A session has an API key entered in its settings, and the environment also has ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set. Which key does an AI call actually use?

options.a: Whichever key was set first
options.b: The session's key — resolution order is request > session > env ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
options.c: The environment variable always wins, since it's the system default
options.d: Both keys are combined into one request

items.feedback_correct: Correct. Key resolution is request > session > env. A per-session key (set during Session Configuration) overrides the environment default; if neither is set, the call fails with a clear 'API key required' error rather than going out silently empty.
items.feedback_incorrect_default: ✗ Resolution order is request > session > env ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. A session-level key you configure takes priority over the environment variable; only when no request or session key is set does the app fall back to the environment default.
